_description: Comprehensive lab reference ranges for adult males. Includes standard clinical ranges and tighter functional/preventive medicine optimal ranges. Used by the Lab Results Interpreter for flagging and trend analysis.

lipid_panel.name: Total Cholesterol
lipid_panel.notes: Borderline high 200-239, high ≥240. Context matters — HDL:LDL ratio is more informative than total alone.

lipid_panel.name: LDL Cholesterol
lipid_panel.notes: Direct LDL preferred over calculated. <70 for high cardiovascular risk. Particle count (LDL-P) is more predictive than LDL-C alone.

lipid_panel.name: HDL Cholesterol
lipid_panel.notes: Higher is generally better for cardiovascular protection. Exercise, omega-3s, and moderate alcohol raise HDL. Very high HDL (>90) may lose protective effect.

lipid_panel.name: Triglycerides
lipid_panel.notes: Must be fasting. <80 is optimal. Highly responsive to diet (sugar, refined carbs, alcohol). Triglyceride:HDL ratio <2 is ideal.

lipid_panel.name: VLDL Cholesterol
lipid_panel.notes: Usually calculated as triglycerides/5. Elevated VLDL correlates with metabolic syndrome.

lipid_panel.name: Total Cholesterol / HDL Ratio
lipid_panel.notes: Better predictor of CVD risk than total cholesterol alone. <3.5 is ideal for men.

metabolic.name: Glucose (Fasting)
metabolic.notes: Must be fasting 8-12 hours. Pre-diabetes: 100-125. Diabetes: ≥126. Functional range 72-86 indicates excellent insulin sensitivity.

metabolic.name: HbA1c
metabolic.notes: 3-month average blood sugar. Pre-diabetes: 5.7-6.4. Diabetes: ≥6.5. <5.2% indicates excellent glycemic control.

metabolic.name: Insulin (Fasting)
metabolic.notes: Fasting insulin is an early marker of insulin resistance — rises before glucose. <8 is optimal. Lab 'normal' range is too wide.

metabolic.name: HOMA-IR
metabolic.notes: Calculated: (fasting glucose × fasting insulin) / 405. <1.0 indicates excellent insulin sensitivity. >2.5 suggests insulin resistance.

metabolic.name: BUN (Blood Urea Nitrogen)
metabolic.notes: Kidney function marker. Can be elevated by high protein intake or dehydration. BUN:Creatinine ratio 10-20:1 is normal.

metabolic.name: Creatinine
metabolic.notes: Kidney function marker. Higher in muscular individuals. Trend is more important than single value.

metabolic.name: eGFR
metabolic.notes: Estimated glomerular filtration rate. >90 is normal. 60-89 is mildly decreased. <60 warrants nephrology referral. Calculated from creatinine.

metabolic.name: Uric Acid
metabolic.notes: Elevated levels associated with gout, kidney stones, and cardiovascular risk. Reduce with limiting purines, fructose, and alcohol.

liver.name: AST (SGOT)
liver.notes: Liver enzyme also found in muscle and heart. Can be transiently elevated after intense exercise. ALT is more liver-specific.

liver.name: ALT (SGPT)
liver.notes: Most liver-specific enzyme. Functional medicine target <26. Elevated by alcohol, medications, fatty liver, and supplements like high-dose niacin.

liver.name: ALP (Alkaline Phosphatase)
liver.notes: Found in liver, bone, and intestine. Low ALP can indicate zinc or magnesium deficiency.

liver.name: GGT (Gamma-GT)
liver.notes: Sensitive marker for bile duct issues and alcohol consumption. Also an independent cardiovascular risk factor. Optimal <30.

liver.name: Bilirubin (Total)
liver.notes: Mild elevation (Gilbert syndrome) is common and benign. Bilirubin is actually an antioxidant. >1.2 with elevated liver enzymes warrants workup.

liver.name: Albumin
liver.notes: Marker of liver synthetic function and nutritional status. Low albumin indicates chronic illness, malnutrition, or liver disease.

thyroid.name: TSH
thyroid.notes: Pituitary hormone — inverse relationship with thyroid hormones. Functional optimal 1.0-2.5. Standard range is too wide; subclinical hypothyroidism often missed.

thyroid.name: Free T4 (Thyroxine)
thyroid.notes: Inactive thyroid hormone. Converted to T3 (active) in peripheral tissues. Mid-range is optimal.

thyroid.name: Free T3 (Triiodothyronine)
thyroid.notes: Active thyroid hormone. Upper half of range is optimal. Low Free T3 with normal TSH may indicate poor T4→T3 conversion (check selenium, zinc, iron).

thyroid.name: Reverse T3
thyroid.notes: Inactive metabolite of T4. Elevated during illness, stress, caloric restriction, and high cortisol. Free T3:Reverse T3 ratio >0.2 is healthy.

thyroid.name: TPO Antibodies
thyroid.notes: Marker for autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's). Elevated antibodies may precede clinical hypothyroidism by years. Recheck annually if positive.

hormones.name: Total Testosterone
hormones.notes: Draw between 7-10 AM when levels peak. Upper half of range is optimal for men. Declines ~1-2% per year after age 30. Support with sleep, exercise, zinc, D3, body composition.

hormones.name: Free Testosterone
hormones.notes: Bioavailable fraction — more clinically relevant than total. Upper half of range is optimal. Low free T with normal total T suggests elevated SHBG.

hormones.name: Estradiol (E2)
hormones.notes: Men need some estradiol for bone health, brain function, and cardiovascular protection. Too low (from aromatase inhibitors) is as problematic as too high.

hormones.name: SHBG
hormones.notes: Sex Hormone Binding Globulin — binds testosterone making it unavailable. Elevated by: hyperthyroidism, low carb diets, aging. Lowered by: obesity, insulin resistance, hypothyroidism.

hormones.name: DHEA-S
hormones.notes: Adrenal androgen precursor. Declines with age. Low levels may indicate adrenal fatigue/insufficiency. Mid-range is optimal.

hormones.name: Cortisol (AM)
hormones.notes: Draw 7-9 AM. Follows circadian rhythm (highest in morning, lowest at midnight). Chronic elevation indicates HPA axis dysfunction. Low AM cortisol suggests adrenal insufficiency.

hormones.name: IGF-1
hormones.notes: Growth hormone mediator. Correlates with GH secretion. Responds to sleep quality, exercise, and protein intake. Very high levels may increase cancer risk.

hormones.name: Prolactin
hormones.notes: Elevated prolactin in men can indicate pituitary adenoma, hypothyroidism, or medication side effect. Inversely related to testosterone.

vitamins_minerals.name: Vitamin D (25-OH)
vitamins_minerals.notes: Most common deficiency worldwide. Lab 'normal' starts at 20 but functional optimal is 40-60. Supplement with D3 (not D2) + K2. Recheck 3 months after dose change.

vitamins_minerals.name: Vitamin B12
vitamins_minerals.notes: Neurological symptoms can occur even within 'normal' range if <500. Methylcobalamin preferred over cyanocobalamin. Check methylmalonic acid (MMA) for functional deficiency.

vitamins_minerals.name: Folate
vitamins_minerals.notes: Important for DNA synthesis and methylation. Check MTHFR status if persistently low despite supplementation. Use methylfolate (5-MTHF) not folic acid.

vitamins_minerals.name: Ferritin
vitamins_minerals.notes: Iron storage protein. Also an acute phase reactant (rises with inflammation). Optimal 50-150 for men. <30 indicates iron deficiency even with normal hemoglobin. >300 warrants hemochromatosis screening.

vitamins_minerals.name: Iron (Serum)
vitamins_minerals.notes: Fluctuates significantly throughout the day and with meals. Best interpreted alongside ferritin, TIBC, and transferrin saturation.

vitamins_minerals.name: TIBC (Total Iron-Binding Capacity)
vitamins_minerals.notes: Rises when iron stores are depleted (body makes more transferrin to capture available iron). Inversely related to ferritin in iron deficiency.

cbc.name: WBC (White Blood Cells)
cbc.notes: Elevated: infection, inflammation, stress, smoking. Low: immunosuppression, autoimmune. Persistent elevation >10 warrants workup.

cbc.name: RBC (Red Blood Cells)
cbc.notes: Low with low hemoglobin = anemia. High (polycythemia) can be caused by dehydration, testosterone therapy, altitude, or smoking.

cbc.name: Hemoglobin
cbc.notes: Oxygen-carrying capacity. Low = anemia. High = polycythemia. Monitor if on TRT — testosterone stimulates erythropoiesis.

cbc.name: Hematocrit
cbc.notes: Percentage of blood volume that is red blood cells. >54% increases clotting risk. Donate blood if chronically elevated (especially on TRT).

cbc.name: MCV (Mean Corpuscular Volume)
cbc.notes: RBC size. Low MCV = microcytic (iron deficiency). High MCV = macrocytic (B12/folate deficiency). Normal MCV doesn't rule out combined deficiency.

cbc.name: Platelets
cbc.notes: Low: bleeding risk, possible ITP. High: reactive (infection, inflammation) or myeloproliferative. Omega-3s may mildly lower platelet count.

inflammation.name: hs-CRP (High-Sensitivity C-Reactive Protein)
inflammation.notes: Systemic inflammation and cardiovascular risk marker. <1.0 low risk, 1-3 moderate, >3 high risk. >10 suggests acute infection (not useful for CVD risk). Reduce with omega-3, exercise, weight loss, statin.

inflammation.name: ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate)
inflammation.notes: Non-specific inflammation marker. Rises with age. Useful for monitoring autoimmune conditions (RA, lupus, PMR). Slower to change than CRP.

inflammation.name: Homocysteine
inflammation.notes: Independent cardiovascular risk factor and methylation marker. Elevated by B12/folate/B6 deficiency and MTHFR mutations. >8 warrants B-vitamin optimization.

electrolytes.name: Sodium
electrolytes.notes: Tightly regulated. Low (hyponatremia): overhydration, SIADH, adrenal insufficiency. High (hypernatremia): dehydration. Critical <130 or >150.

electrolytes.name: Potassium
electrolytes.notes: Critical for cardiac rhythm. Both hypo- and hyperkalemia are dangerous. Hemolyzed samples give falsely elevated results. Recheck if unexpected.

electrolytes.name: Magnesium (RBC)
electrolytes.notes: RBC magnesium is far more accurate than serum magnesium (which remains normal until severely depleted). Subclinical deficiency is extremely common. Involved in 300+ enzymatic reactions.

electrolytes.name: Calcium (Total)
electrolytes.notes: Adjust for albumin: corrected calcium = total calcium + 0.8 × (4.0 - albumin). Elevated calcium: hyperparathyroidism, malignancy, excess D3.

electrolytes.name: Phosphorus
electrolytes.notes: Inversely related to calcium. Low phosphorus can cause muscle weakness and bone pain. High phosphorus with low calcium suggests kidney disease.
